passage:
Vinita, 9:40 pm: tejas did u see?? board is removing the choice questions from maths this year 😰
Tejas: says who
Vinita: literally everyone. 5 pages posted it. my cousin's page too
Vinita: if 5 pages say it it's real na
Tejas: send them
Vinita: [five screenshots]
Tejas: look at the bottom of each one
Tejas: same spelling mistake. "questons"
Tejas: same blue background, same clock emoji in the corner
Vinita: ...
Tejas: that's one post copied 5 times. not 5 people who checked
Vinita: ok but it still FEELS true. i've seen it all day
Vinita: and i already told my whole tuition group 😅
Tejas: check the board's own site tonight. then tell them
Vinita: fine. but if it's true you're buying me chai
Tejas: deal 👍

qa.q: What spelling mistake did Tejas spot at the bottom of each screenshot?
qa.a: "questons", the same spelling mistake on each one.

qa.q: Why does the claim still "FEEL true" to Vinita after seeing the copies?
qa.a: Vinita had seen it all day across five pages and had already repeated it, so it felt solid even after learning it was one post copied five times.

qa.q: What does Tejas suggest before Vinita tells the tuition group anything more, and why is that the right step?
qa.a: Check the board's own site tonight. One official source counts for more than five copies of the same post.

qa.q: How might Vinita's tuition group be affected by the message Vinita already sent?
qa.a: They may start worrying and changing how they revise over a claim that might be false, and the rumour could spread further through them.

grounding: A teenager accepts a claim seen on several pages until a friend shows they all copied one original post.

passage: By Tuesday night Farida had seen the leopard clip five times: on the town news page, on two cricket-club accounts, on her cousin's status and on a page called Our Kasba Updates. Each caption said the same thing: "spotted near canal road, stay aleart." Farida lay on her charpai with the phone, heart jumping. The canal road was her road to school. Next morning she told Nandini, "Everyone's posting it. It must be true." Nandini took the phone and scrolled slowly. "Look. Same clip, same shaky tree, same time in the corner. Even the same spelling of 'aleart'." She tapped the oldest post. "They all copied this one." Farida read the caption again. It sounded just as true as before, which annoyed her. They walked the canal road together anyway, past the tea stall where the forest guard was laughing with the owner about "that old video".

qa.q: Where had Farida seen the leopard clip?
qa.a: On the town news page, two cricket-club accounts, her cousin's status and a page called Our Kasba Updates.

qa.q: Why was Farida annoyed after Nandini showed that the posts were copies?
qa.a: The caption still sounded just as true as before, even though she now knew all five came from one post, and that gap between knowing and feeling bothered her.

qa.q: What did Nandini do that Farida could use the next time a claim is everywhere?
qa.a: Scroll slowly, compare the posts and find the oldest one. If they share the same clip and spelling, it is one claim repeated, not five sightings.

qa.q: How might the forest guard see the rumour?
qa.a: The guard laughs about "that old video", which suggests it is a familiar recycled clip rather than a real sighting near the canal road.

grounding: A small-town teenager starts believing a leopard sighting because five accounts shared it, though all copied one post.

passage: Wei first saw it on Sunday: "City to ban phones in every high school from March!" By Wednesday it had turned up on a meme page, a gaming account, two classmates' stories and a video with dramatic music. Each time it felt a little more settled, like the weather. On Thursday at dinner in their Vancouver apartment, Wei announced it as fact. "Everyone's saying it." Xin, home from university for the weekend, asked, "Who said it first?" Wei shrugged. "Doesn't matter. It's everywhere." Xin scrolled for two minutes and turned the screen round. Every version linked back to one post from a joke news site, the kind that invents headlines for fun. The meme page had cropped off the joke label. Wei stared, then laughed a little too loudly. "I told my whole class," Wei said. "Now I have to untell them."

qa.q: Where did every version of the claim lead back to?
qa.a: One post from a joke news site, the kind that invents headlines for fun.

qa.q: How did Wei feel on seeing where the claim came from, and what shows it?
qa.a: Embarrassed 😅 Wei stared, laughed a little too loudly and remembered telling the whole class.

qa.q: Which question from Xin changed things, and how could Wei use it in future?
qa.a: "Who said it first?" Wei could trace a claim to its first post before sharing it, instead of trusting that it is everywhere.

qa.q: How might Wei's classmates feel when Wei has to "untell" them?
qa.a: Some may feel relieved and some a bit silly for believing it, and they may trust Wei more for correcting it honestly.

grounding: A teenager accepts a headline seen across many accounts until a sibling traces every copy back to one joke post.

passage: The hostel common room at the residential school outside Dehradun went quiet at nine, except for phones. Mohit, fifteen, had seen it six times since dinner: "Board order: hostel wifi shut from 9 pm for all Class 10 from Monday." A meme page, a quiz account, two seniors' stories, a video with sad music, a page that said NEWS in red. By the sixth, he stopped wondering and started downloading every chemistry video he might need. Sudha, from his class, looked over. "Scroll to the corner of each one." Mohit did. Every picture had the same tiny faded logo, from one joke page. The five others had just copied it. "Oh," he said. He'd been so sure. He kept downloading anyway, slower now, half laughing at himself.

qa.q: How many times had Mohit seen the wifi claim since dinner?
qa.a: He had seen it six times.

qa.q: Why did Mohit stop wondering after the sixth post?
qa.a: Seeing the same claim on so many accounts made it feel settled, as if six places meant six separate sources.

qa.q: What check could Mohit use the next time a claim shows up everywhere?
qa.a: He could look for where each post came from, like Sudha's tip about the logo, before accepting it.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel about pointing out the logo to Mohit?
qa.a: Sudha might feel a bit pleased to help, and hopeful that Mohit will stop panicking over a joke page.

grounding: A teen accepts a claim seen on six accounts, not noticing all copied one original post.

passage:
Dear Ramesh Bhaiya,
You'll laugh, but I need to tell someone who won't tell Mummy.
Okay, I did tell Mummy. That's the problem.
Last week I saw a post saying all schools in our district would get three extra weeks of summer holiday because of the heat. Then I saw it again on a cricket page. Then on my friend's status. Then on four more accounts. By the seventh time it felt like a notice from the principal. I told Mummy we could finally visit you in Nagpur, and she even started asking about train tickets.
Yesterday Sir laughed in class and showed us where it came from: one parody account. Everyone else had just copied it, word for word.
I feel so silly. Seven times felt like seven proofs. It was one joke, seven times.
Jatin

qa.q: Where did the holiday post really come from?
qa.a: It came from one parody account, and everyone else had copied it word for word.

qa.q: What does Jatin mean by "Seven times felt like seven proofs"?
qa.a: Jatin means seeing the claim on many accounts made it feel checked, even though it was really one source repeated.

qa.q: What turning point could help Jatin next time, and how?
qa.a: The moment Sir traced the post to one account; next time Jatin could look for the original before telling Mummy anything.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel after asking about train tickets?
qa.a: She may feel a little foolish or disappointed, though likely amused too, since Jatin believed it honestly.

grounding: A teen accepts a claim after seeing it on many accounts, not realising they all copied one post.
